header:
Date: 2027-02-25
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (CTO - Cerulean), Raj Singh (Head of Infra), Priya Kumar (Security), Omar Velasquez (DevOps)
Recording: Fireflies auto-transcript (some mislabels expected)
topics: Private/VPC deployment options; VPC peering vs Transit Gateway; private endpoints and DNS; cross-account peering; CIDR overlap; region constraints and multi-region strategy; latency/cost tradeoffs; security/compliance (KMS, SOC2, audit logs); next steps for pilot and benchmarks
summary: Cerulean is evaluating Redwood Private deployment (VPC) to host inference for low-latency customer-facing features. Key concerns: how network connectivity will work (peering vs TGW), CIDR overlap with existing VPCs, private endpoints for control plane and model pull, cross-region considerations (eu-west-1 requirement), auditability and KMS integration. Redwood AE/SE explained architecture options, tradeoffs, and proposed next steps: share network checklist, run benchmark, share security docs, and provide pricing estimate.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick roll call — i'll start, maya chen from redwood AE. arjun is our se.
[00:08] Arjun Patel: hi all, arjun patel, i focus on private deployments and network setup.
[00:12] Lena Ortiz: lena here, cerulean cto. thanks for doing this. we want to understand private option and if we can keep traffic inside our vpc.
[00:18] Raj Singh: raj, infra. our main questions are around peering, transit gateway, and how control plane talks to our network.
[00:22] Priya Kumar: priya, security. i'll focus on compliance, kms and logging.
[00:25] Maya Chen: perfect. agenda: quick product overview for private/vpc, network patterns (peering vs tgw), cross-region concerns, security/compliance, and then next steps. sound good?
[00:33] Lena Ortiz: yes.
[00:35] Arjun Patel: quick note — apologies if i mispronounce anything, auto transcript may mess up names.
[00:38] Maya Chen: cool. so at a high level redwood private runs the inference control plane in your account or in a customer-managed vpc depending on the option. we have two common patterns: cross-account private endpoints where redwood control plane sits in a managed VPC with private endpoints into your VPC, or a customer-hosted model where we deploy a private control plane entirely inside your VPCs — both support pinned model versions and dedicated capacity.
[01:02] Raj Singh: can you explain the peering vs transit gateway difference in practice? we have dozens of VPCs and don't want a million peering connections.
[01:10] Arjun Patel: totally. so peering is direct vpc-to-vpc, good for a few links. transit gateway (tgw) scales better for many vpcs; you can attach multiple accounts and use central routing. for cerulean i'd recommend tgw if you plan to connect 10+ vpcs; otherwise a cross-account peering plus route tables is fine.
[01:28] Lena Ortiz: okay. what about cidr overlap? we have some legacy ranges that cause overlap with partners.
[01:33] Maya Chen: overlap is a common blocker. our network checklist asks for all VPC CIDR ranges and subnets up front. if overlap exists we have a couple options: use NAT/proxy and run inference in a separate VPC with non-overlapping CIDR, or set up AWS PrivateLink endpoints from our managed VPC into yours so you don't need peering; PrivateLink avoids route-level overlap because it's endpoint-based.
[01:56] Raj Singh: interesting — how does privatelink compare to tgw from a security/audit standpoint?
[02:02] Arjun Patel: PrivateLink is more restrictive — it's an elastic network interface-backed endpoint in your subnet, so traffic doesn't traverse the public internet and you can apply security groups. Transit gateway gives more flexibility for east-west connectivity but is more complex. from audit perspective both can be instrumented — we can forward flow logs, VPC flow logs, and our control plane emits audit events to your logging collector if required.
[02:26] Priya Kumar: you mentioned the control plane — does it ever hold customer data? our compliance needs say control plane should not retain PII and keys must be in our KMS.
[02:35] Maya Chen: good question. the default is that the control plane handles orchestration metadata; customer payloads and artifacts (trained model artifacts, prompt logs) can be configured to remain in your VPC or S3 under your account. for KMS we integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping on private deployments; with HSM support available for enterprise customers. we'll share the KMS integration doc.
[02:56] Lena Ortiz: region constraints — we have eu-west-1 customers; can you run private in eu-west-1?
[03:00] Arjun Patel: yes, we support private deployments in multiple regions. for eu-west-1 we'll deploy dedicated capacity in that region; note that some of our managed services (control plane or metrics) may be in a central region unless you opt for full private control plane inside your VPC which keeps everything in region. we'll outline the tradeoffs in the doc.
[03:21] Raj Singh: latency — we expect sub-50ms for small prompt workloads. is that achievable with the private option?
[03:26] Arjun Patel: with an in-vpc deployment it's very achievable — latency depends on instance type and model. for smaller LLMs (quantized) we've seen 20-40ms p50 in-region. dedicated capacity helps with predictable latency; hosted API will add network hop. we'll propose a benchmark with your typical prompt distribution.
[03:46] Omar Velasquez: about egress — if instances need to pull from external registries, how do you manage outbound? we prefer to avoid public internet egress.
[03:53] Maya Chen: we can pull images/artifacts from your private artifact repo or mirror registries into your VPC. we also support S3 endpoints for model artifacts; for initial onboarding we may request temporary access but long-term everything can be in your private subnets.
[04:07] Priya Kumar: what about audit logs and traceability — we need immutable logs for model inference events tied to request IDs.
[04:13] Arjun Patel: our runtime emits per-request trace IDs and audit events. for private deployments we can ship logs directly to your ELK/Datadog/Splunk via a VPC endpoint or put logs into your S3 bucket with server-side encryption using your KMS. we also support request-level sampling if volume is too high.
[04:32] Lena Ortiz: nice. competitors — have you seen customers move from anthro or openai hosted to private redwood? any pitfalls?
[04:38] Maya Chen: yes, a few customers migrated for data residency and egress control. common pitfalls: CIDR overlap, not accounting for control plane endpoints in firewall rules, and underestimating the amount of flow logs/metrics egress. we help with a checklist to avoid those.
[04:56] Raj Singh: can you talk about authentication — how do we authenticate requests into the inference cluster?
[05:01] Arjun Patel: you can use mTLS with client certs, or short-lived tokens issued by your identity provider. we integrate with SAML/SSO for the console and also support IAM roles for cross-account assume-role flows when needed.
[05:15] Priya Kumar: do you support SCIM or SSO provisioning for our org?
[05:18] Maya Chen: yes, enterprise customers can use SAML + SCIM provisioning for user management.
[05:22] Omar Velasquez: what's the onboarding timeline for private in-vpc? we're trying to schedule for q2 production readiness.
[05:28] Maya Chen: typical timeline is 4-8 weeks for private in-vpc depending on complexity — faster if you already have a TGW and non-overlapping CIDRs. Dedicated managed option (redwood-managed but VPC peering) usually is 2-4 weeks. we'll include a sample timeline.
[05:41] Lena Ortiz: pricing — high level estimate now is fine. we want to compare dedicated vs private fully managed.
[05:47] Maya Chen: we'll provide a preliminary estimate in the follow-up. key levers are reserved capacity hours, instance types, and egress/storage.
[05:54] Raj Singh: network routing specifics — do you require route table modifications or only endpoints?
[05:59] Arjun Patel: depends on pattern. with peering you must add route table entries for the peered CIDR. with PrivateLink you create an endpoint service and we create an endpoint in your subnet — route tables are largely unchanged but security groups and NACLs matter.
[06:13] Priya Kumar: what about cross-account IAM — do we need to give redwood accounts any IAM permissions?
[06:17] Maya Chen: for cross-account setups we request a narrow assume-role with least privilege to manage the redwood infra components; for customer-hosted we deploy using a CloudFormation/terraform bundle and you control the IAM roles. we'll provide templates.
[06:30] Lena Ortiz: can you show a sample network diagram?
[06:33] Arjun Patel: yes — i'll attach an example in the follow-up: three patterns: 1) PrivateLink into a redwood-managed control plane, 2) cross-account peering with redwood-managed nodes in our account, 3) full in-vpc control plane and nodes. each shows subnets for mgmt, inference, and observability, with flows for logs to your storage.
[06:53] Raj Singh: about observability — will the control plane send metrics out-of-band or do we pull?
[06:58] Arjun Patel: we can push metrics using your metrics endpoint via VPC endpoint or write them to your S3/CloudWatch. many customers prefer us to push to their ingest endpoint for central observability.
[07:08] Maya Chen: quick checkpoint — any other hard blockers we should know about?
[07:12] Raj Singh: CIDR overlap and eu-west-1 residency are the main blockers. also need assurance on kms key usage.
[07:18] Priya Kumar: also retention policies — we need to define retention of logs and prompt traces.
[07:22] Maya Chen: understood. for retention we can configure data retention at deployment time and export logs to your long-term store.
[07:27] Lena Ortiz: security question — can we run inference nodes in private subnets with no internet egress and still get updates?
[07:33] Arjun Patel: yes — you'll need a controlled egress path or an artifact mirror. we support pulling container images from a private registry in your VPC or via an S3 bucket and lifecycle hooks to update nodes without public internet.
[07:47] Omar Velasquez: about certificates and rotation — do you manage cert rotation for mTLS or do we?
[07:52] Maya Chen: we can manage cert rotation or integrate with your cert manager. in private setups customers often prefer to manage certs; we can provide automation scripts.
[07:59] Raj Singh: what about multi-region active-active? we have users in us-west and eu-west and want geo-routing.
[08:05] Arjun Patel: supported. active-active requires model replication and synchronization of KV/cache state; we usually recommend stateful routing per region with a smart router that can route by latency or customer region and fall back to another region if needed. there are tradeoffs for KV cache warming and consistency.
[08:25] Lena Ortiz: ok. can you outline the specific network artifacts you need from us?
[08:29] Maya Chen: yes — network checklist: VPC IDs and CIDR ranges, list of subnets (public/private) and AZs, route tables, security group baseline, any TGW attachments, egress/firewall rules, allowed ports, proxy requirements, and preferred registry/S3 locations for artifacts. also whether you prefer PrivateLink or TGW.
[08:49] Raj Singh: we'll collate that.
[08:51] Maya Chen: great. i'll read back next steps and responsibilities.
[08:54] Maya Chen: next steps: maya to send network checklist and example diagrams; arjun to propose benchmark plan; cerulean to share CIDR and region requirements; priya to send compliance questions.
[09:02] Priya Kumar: timeline-wise we want the benchmark in march and decision by end of q2.
[09:07] Maya Chen: perfect. any other quick q's?
[09:09] Lena Ortiz: nothing else from me.
[09:11] Raj Singh: nope.
[09:12] Arjun Patel: i'll include sample terraform cloudformation snippets, and a checklist for ports and flow logs.
[09:18] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with docs and schedule the deep-dive.
[09:21] Lena Ortiz: thanks. bye.
[09:23] (call ends)
